a: the disease, the sword and the famine
t: Is the famine in the list?
p: A Qumran copy of the long text lacks "the famine" in this list; the Masoretic Text and the Greek have all three.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); the Greek has all three, in the order death, famine, sword (Swete's text)

readings.w: 4QJer-c (4Q72), as transcribed by Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC); the words for "the disease" are restored, the others visible
readings.en: from the disease and from the sword

why: The Masoretic Text has the support of the Greek, and the stock triad of sword, famine and disease runs through the book (24:10; 14:12). The scroll's shorter list may well be a copyist's skip, since "from the ... and from the ..." repeats.
b: The three-part list appears again in verse 9 ("by the sword, by famine and by disease"), where 4QJer-c does have the famine ("and by famine"), which makes a slip in verse 7 more likely than a different edition.

a: I am setting
p: The Masoretic Text has a participle, "I am putting"; 4QJer-c and the Greek have a past tense, "I have put."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008)
4QJer-c (4Q72; "Look" and the verb visible, "I" restored); the Greek has "I have given" (Swete's text)

why: The Masoretic Text is kept. The two readings differ little in meaning: the choice of life or death is already placed before the people. Two independent witnesses (a scroll and the Greek) agree on the past tense, so it is a real alternative.

a: Who can come down on us?
p: The Hebrew has "come down on us" (yachat); Swete's Greek has "terrify us."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008)

readings.plain: Who can come down on us?

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus

why: The Hebrew is kept. The two readings differ only in the verb: yachat from nachat ("come down") against a verb from chatat ("be terrified, terrify"). The Greek may read the same letters as the second verb. The sense is close: no one can break into the hiding places.
b: No scroll preserves this verse.

a: cedar
p: Swete's Greek reads "Ahaz your father" where the Hebrew has "cedar."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); 4QJer-a (4Q70) and 4QJer-c (4Q72) both preserve "in cedar"
Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus

why: The two scrolls and the Hebrew agree, and the Greek looks like a misreading: the Hebrew letters for "cedar" (ארז) and "Ahaz" (אחז) differ by one letter. Ahaz was not Jehoiakim's father; Josiah was.

p: A Qumran copy has "poured out" where the Masoretic Text and the Greek have "broken."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); the Greek has "were crushed" (Swete's text)
4QJer-c (4Q72), a clear reading

why: Two witnesses (the Masoretic Text and the Greek) read "broken." The scroll's "poured out" changes two letters (a pe for the bet, a kaf for the resh) and looks like a slip, though it makes sense: allies spilled out and gone.
b: The same scroll also reads "in Lebanon" (בלבנון) for "Lebanon" (הלבנון) earlier in the verse.

a: how you will be pitied
p: The Masoretic Text has "how you will be pitied" (nechant); Swete's Greek has "you will groan."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); 4QJer-c (4Q72) has the same consonants, nchnt, visible ("how" before it is restored)
readings.en: how you will be pitied (a passive of chanan, "show favor")

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus; the same sense could come from a Hebrew ne'enachet (from anach, "sigh")

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which the scroll supports. The form nechant is rare and hard, and "groan" is the easy sense, so the Greek may have smoothed it or read a different Hebrew word; only the Greek supports it. Either way the line speaks of the pain of childbirth coming on the proud city.

a: stripped of children
p: The Hebrew says "childless" or "stripped of children"; Swete's Greek says the man is to be written down as "proclaimed out" (outlawed).

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008)
Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew 'ariri, which is rare. It appears in Genesis 15:2 (Abram "going childless") and in Leviticus 20:20-21, where being without children is a punishment. The Greek word means someone cried out of the community, which may be the translator's guess.
b: The word does not say Jeconiah had no children at all: 1 Chronicles 3:17-18 names sons, and Babylonian ration tablets list five of his sons. It describes a man with no heir who will rule, or who loses his children as the Hebrew idiom suggests. The Greek goes on to say that no one from his seed will "grow up" sitting on David's throne.

a: The LORD is our righteousness
t: The LORD is our righteousness, or Jehozadak?
p: Swete's Greek gives the name as "Josedek" (Jehozadak), the name of the priest who was Joshua's father.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008)
Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus

why: The Masoretic Text is kept: it matches the later copy of the oracle (33:16) and plays on Zedekiah's name. The Greek form reads like a transcription of the Hebrew name yehotsadaq ("the LORD has made righteous"), the name of the high priest in Haggai 1:1 and 1 Chronicles 6:15.
b: Jehozadak was the father of Joshua the high priest, who is the "Branch" figure of Zechariah 3:8 and 6:11-12. Some see a link in the Greek; it is not necessary to explain the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew reads "What oracle?"; the Greek, and Rashi, read the same letters as "You are the burden."

p: The pointed Hebrew says "forget" (nashah); the Greek has "I take you up and dash you down."

Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus

readings.plain: take you up and dash you down

why: The Hebrew is kept as pointed. The two readings differ only in the verb: nashah "forget" and nasa' "lift." The Greek takes the second, which fits the play on massa' ("burden," from nasa') in the verses before; but the Hebrew may be a deliberate pun on both verbs.

a: serve the king of Babylon
p: The Greek says the people will serve "among the nations"; the Hebrew says they will serve the king of Babylon.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008)
readings.orig: וְעָבְדוּ הַגּוֹיִם הָאֵלֶּה אֶת מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus

why: The Masoretic Text is kept; "the king of Babylon" is the clear object in 27:7 and 29:10, and the seventy years are tied to Babylon. The Greek reads as if the people are exiles in many countries.
b: This affects how the seventy years are counted: Babylon's own era in the Hebrew, a general exile in the Greek.

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which ends the verse with this clause and uses it as the bridge to the nation oracles in chapters 46-51. The Greek has the clause too, but as the title of a block of oracles that follows at once, so its position and its "all" differ. Scholars divide on whether the Greek keeps an earlier arrangement (Tov, Bogaert) or rearranged the book.
b: Swete numbers the heading 25:14, so his verse numbers here differ from the Hebrew's (the Hebrew 25:14 has no match, see the next entry). The Greek 25:13 itself ends with "all that is written in this book," as the Hebrew does, and the nation oracles follow, starting with Elam (Greek 25:14-31:44 in Swete's numbering).

b: 4QJer-c has only restored words in this verse ("who live" and "in the wilderness" are both in brackets), so the scroll gives no evidence here, either way.

a: all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam and all the kings of Media
p: The Greek has "the kings of Elam and the kings of the Persians"; it lacks Zimri and Media. 4QJer-c shows Zimri.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); 4QJer-c (4Q72) has "all the kings of Zimri" and the third "all the kings of" visible; "Elam" and "Media" are restored
readings.plain: all the kings of Zimri, all the kings of Elam and all the kings of Media

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus (Greek 32:11)
readings.plain: all the kings of Elam and all the kings of the Persians

why: The Masoretic Text is kept. The scroll shows that Zimri was already in the Hebrew list, so the Greek's shorter list is not simply the older one. The scroll does not prove Media, since its name is restored. The Greek's "Persians" is a more recent name for the same region and may be an update by the translator or his source.

a: all the kings of the north, near and far
p: Swete's Greek has "all the kings from the east, near and far"; the Hebrew and 4QJer-c have "the north."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); 4QJer-c (4Q72) preserves "the north"
readings.plain: all the kings of the north, near and far

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus (Greek 32:12, ἀπὸ ἀπηλιώτου)
readings.plain: all the kings from the east, near and far

why: Two witnesses (the Masoretic Text and the scroll) read "north." The Greek's "from the east" has no obvious Hebrew behind it.

a: And the king of Sheshach will drink after them.
p: The Greek lacks the sentence about the king of Sheshach; 4QJer-c has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); 4QJer-c (4Q72) preserves "the king of Sheshach will drink"
readings.en: and the king of Sheshach will drink after them
readings.plain: And the king of Sheshach will drink after them.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, the full Hebrew text. The Greek here is shorter, and scholars divide on whether it translates an earlier, shorter Hebrew edition (Tov, Bogaert) or whether its translator or his source cut the text. Where a Qumran copy of the longer text survives it is named; it shows only that the longer text already existed.
b: The shorter Greek here is a case where a scroll shows the longer text already existed. Some scholars argue the Greek translator dropped the cipher as unintelligible; others think the cipher was added to a shorter text.

a: fall like a precious vessel
p: Swete's Greek has "fall like the choice rams" and lacks "your scattering."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008)
readings.en: and you will fall like a precious vessel

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus (Greek 32:20)

why: The Hebrew is kept; the broken fine vessel matches the smashed jar of 22:28. The Greek has made the whole verse a figure of the flock, consistently with "rams" for "lords of the flock" earlier in the verse.
b: The Hebrew also says "and your scattering" (tefotsotekhem), a word that is hard to explain; some change it to "I will shatter you" (compare the Greek, which lacks it).

a: the oppressor's fierce anger
t: The oppressor's anger, or the great sword?
p: Swete's Greek has "the great sword."

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008)
readings.en: the fierce anger of the oppressor

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's edition, Codex Vaticanus (Greek 32:24)

why: The Hebrew is kept. "The sword of the oppressor" (cherev hayyonah) occurs at 46:16 and 50:16, and the Greek's "sword" may reflect that phrase, which suggests a change of one letter from "anger" (charon) to "sword" (cherev) in 25:38.
